# The register rules: Anima

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Anima, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Anima to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **ANIMA**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Anima**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: 'AH-nih-mah' — stress the first syllable; the middle vowel is short and light. The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *anima* differs from the canonical *Anima* only by convention of display — case, not content. It is *acceptable everywhere*: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. The Latin anima overlaps with Greek psychē, Hebrew nephesh, Sanskrit ātman, and Greek pneuma.  All of these terms begin with breath or wind and develop into concepts of soul, spirit, or self.

And it never stopped working. Anima is one of the most quietly influential words in Western languages.  It underlies 'animal' (a being that has breath), 'animate' (to give life), 'animation' (the illusion of life in images), and 'animism' (the attribution of soul to natural objects).

## The Convention's Own History

The marks this register defends were not invented for typesetting. Ancient Greek carried a melodic pitch accent, and the acute and circumflex were added by Alexandrian scholars — Aristophanes of Byzantium, tradition holds — precisely to preserve it when the spoken language began to level. Vowel quantity (the macron's concern) is older still: it changes meter, meaning, and grammar, and the poets of the Theogony depend on it. To drop either class of mark is to drop two millennia of deliberate preservation. The restored-stress convention simply continues the oldest documented project in European scholarship: keeping the sound of Greek alive in its letters.

## Where Protocol Meets Practice

The technical answer is simple: the canonical marks are legal IDNA 2008 characters, encoded as punycode under `xn--`. The practical answer is messier: legal does not mean stocked (registrar inventory is partial), and stocked does not mean typeable (stacked diacritics defeat mobile keyboards).

So the register's rule is a hierarchy of attested forms — full restoration, circumflex, macron-only, attested variant, and finally plain ASCII for the systems that cannot carry marks. Every rung is defensible because every rung is attested. The forms this register rules against are not rungs; they are errors, and errors do not get rungs.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Anima** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *anima* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Anima** stands at [/anima/](/anima/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 6 cited sources — Oxford Latin Dictionary, s.v. anima, Lewis and Short, A Latin Dictionary, s.v. anima, Cicero, De natura deorum and Tusculanae disputationes.
